### Problem Statement

Healthcare organizations implementing event-driven microservices architectures face significant challenges in tracing and debugging distributed workflows that span multiple services and message brokers. A single business transaction—such as processing a medical claim involving 8 microservices (Claim Intake, Eligibility Verification, Benefits Calculation, Pricing, Provider Network, Payment Processing, Notification, and Audit Logging)—generates dozens of events flowing through Kafka topics with no unified view of the complete workflow. When claim processing fails or experiences delays (affecting 5-8% of the 1.5M monthly claims), operations teams spend 2-4 hours manually correlating logs across services to identify which service failed, at what step, and why. Without distributed tracing infrastructure, organizations struggle with: inability to visualize end-to-end request flows across service boundaries (logs scattered across 50+ microservices), lack of correlation between events published to Kafka and consumed by downstream services (no way to trace claim ID C123 from intake through payment), performance bottlenecks hidden in distributed workflows (eligibility verification taking 8 seconds but unclear which upstream dependency causes delay), cascading failures where one service failure impacts multiple workflows (provider service down affects claim processing, prior authorizations, and member enrollment simultaneously), and inadequate troubleshooting tools requiring manual log aggregation from multiple sources. The absence of distributed tracing results in: 2-4 hour mean time to resolution (MTTR) for production incidents, 15-20% of engineering time spent on manual log correlation and troubleshooting, inability to proactively identify performance degradation before customer impact, compliance audit challenges with no end-to-end audit trail for HIPAA transactions, and customer service escalations when workflows fail silently without alerts.

### Solution Overview

The Infrastructure Event Tracing pattern implements distributed tracing across event-driven microservices using OpenTelemetry for instrumentation and Jaeger for trace visualization. Every service participating in distributed workflows is instrumented to create, propagate, and collect trace context (trace ID, span ID, parent span ID) through event payloads and HTTP headers. When a business transaction begins (claim submitted to API Gateway), the system generates a unique trace ID that flows through all services and events, creating a hierarchical tree of spans representing each operation. The pattern implements: Trace Context Propagation where services inject trace context into Kafka event headers and HTTP requests, ensuring correlation across service boundaries; OpenTelemetry Instrumentation providing auto-instrumentation for Spring Boot applications (automatic span creation for HTTP requests, Kafka producers/consumers, database calls, external API invocations) and custom spans for business-critical operations (claim adjudication logic, eligibility determination, pricing calculations); Jaeger Backend for collecting trace data from services (via OpenTelemetry Collector), storing traces in Cassandra for 30-day retention, and providing web UI for trace search and visualization; Trace Sampling Strategies balancing observability (trace 100% of errors and slow requests > 5 seconds) with cost (sample 1-5% of successful requests to reduce data volume); Service Mesh Integration where Istio or Linkerd provide automatic trace propagation for service-to-service HTTP communication without code changes. This comprehensive tracing enables: End-to-end workflow visibility with interactive flamegraph showing claim processing flow from intake (2ms) → eligibility (850ms) → benefits (1.2s) → pricing (3.4s) → payment (620ms); Root cause analysis within minutes by drilling into failed spans (eligibility verification span shows 500 error from external payer API with 30-second timeout); Performance optimization through P95/P99 latency analysis per service (identified pricing service as bottleneck consuming 60% of total claim processing time); Dependency mapping automatically generating service dependency graphs (claims service depends on eligibility, benefits, pricing, provider network, notification services).

### When to Use

**Ideal Scenarios:**

- **Event-Driven Microservices**: Distributed systems using message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SNS/SQS) where business workflows span 3+ services publishing and consuming events (claim processing involving 8 services, member enrollment spanning 5 services, prior authorization workflow across 6 services)
- **Complex Request Flows**: Multi-hop workflows where requests traverse multiple service boundaries with synchronous (REST/gRPC) and asynchronous (event-driven) communication patterns (claim submission → API Gateway → Claims Service → Kafka → Eligibility Service → External Payer API → Kafka → Benefits Service)
- **Performance Troubleshooting**: Systems experiencing latency issues where bottlenecks are hidden in distributed call chains (P95 claim processing latency 12 seconds but unclear which of 8 services contributes most delay)
- **Production Incident Resolution**: Environments where MTTR needs improvement and manual log correlation is time-consuming (current 2-4 hour MTTR for claim processing failures, target < 30 minutes)
- **Compliance and Audit Requirements**: Healthcare workflows requiring complete audit trails for regulatory compliance (HIPAA requires tracking all access to protected health information across system boundaries, audit trail must show which services accessed member data during claim adjudication)

**Required Conditions:**

- Microservices architecture with 5+ services communicating via REST APIs and/or message brokers (distributed tracing overhead not justified for monolithic applications)
- Infrastructure for running distributed tracing backend (Jaeger requires Cassandra/Elasticsearch cluster for trace storage, OpenTelemetry Collector for data collection, Kubernetes cluster for deployment)
- Engineering commitment to instrument services (adding OpenTelemetry SDK dependencies, propagating trace context through custom code where auto-instrumentation insufficient)
- Acceptable performance overhead (OpenTelemetry adds 1-3ms latency per traced operation, trace sampling reduces overhead for high-volume services)

**NOT Recommended When:**

- **Monolithic Applications**: Single-process applications where standard logging and APM tools (Datadog APM, New Relic) provide sufficient visibility without distributed tracing complexity
- **Simple Service Architectures**: Systems with 2-3 services where request flows are straightforward and easily understood through traditional logging
- **Resource-Constrained Environments**: Organizations lacking infrastructure to run Jaeger backend (Cassandra cluster, OpenTelemetry Collectors) or unwilling to accept 10-15% infrastructure cost increase for observability
- **Batch Processing Systems**: Non-real-time workflows processing data in large batches where individual request tracing provides limited value (nightly ETL jobs better monitored with batch metrics and job-level logging)

### Benefits

**Operational Efficiency:**
- **85% reduction in MTTR** (2-4 hours → 15-30 minutes for production incidents through instant root cause identification via trace visualization instead of manual log correlation)
- **60% reduction in troubleshooting time** (engineering team spends 15-20% of time troubleshooting → 6-8% with distributed tracing providing immediate visibility into failures)
- **Proactive issue detection** (identify performance degradation before customer impact through P95/P99 latency alerting per service, detect cascading failures through dependency analysis)

**Performance Optimization:**
- **Identify bottlenecks immediately** (flamegraph visualization shows pricing service consuming 60% of claim processing duration, optimization reduces P95 from 12s → 6s)
- **Optimize critical paths** (trace analysis reveals eligibility verification performs redundant database queries, caching optimization reduces latency from 850ms → 200ms)
- **Data-driven capacity planning** (trace metrics show payment service at 70% CPU under load, inform horizontal scaling decisions before performance degrades)

**Developer Productivity:**
- **Faster development cycles** (developers test locally with trace visualization, immediately see impact of code changes on distributed workflows)
- **Improved code quality** (trace spans reveal inefficient patterns like N+1 queries, chatty service-to-service communication, excessive retries)
- **Better onboarding** (new developers visualize system behavior through traces, understand service interactions faster than reading documentation)

**Compliance and Audit:**
- **Complete audit trails** (every claim processing workflow traced end-to-end, satisfies HIPAA requirement for tracking PHI access across services)
- **Security investigation support** (trace suspicious activity patterns like unusual access sequences, identify compromised service accounts through abnormal trace patterns)
- **Regulatory reporting** (generate compliance reports showing service-level access to member data, demonstrate segregation of duties through trace analysis)

### Business Context

A Medicaid managed care organization serving 8 million members across 6 state contracts operates 50+ microservices processing 1.5 million medical claims, 500,000 prior authorizations, and 250,000 member enrollments monthly. The platform migrated from monolithic architecture to event-driven microservices using Kafka for asynchronous communication and REST APIs for synchronous requests. Core business workflows span multiple service boundaries:

**Claim Processing Workflow** (8 services, 45-second average duration):
- Claims Service receives EDI 837 claim submission from provider portal
- Publishes ClaimReceivedEvent to Kafka topic
- Eligibility Service consumes event, verifies member coverage on date of service
- Publishes EligibilityVerifiedEvent
- Benefits Service calculates member cost-sharing (deductibles, copays, coinsurance)
- Publishes BenefitsCalculatedEvent
- Pricing Service applies fee schedules and contract rates
- Publishes PricingCompletedEvent
- Provider Network Service validates provider participation and network status
- Publishes ProviderVerifiedEvent
- Payment Service generates payment (check or EFT), updates ledger
- Publishes PaymentProcessedEvent
- Notification Service sends remittance advice to provider
- Audit Service logs complete claim adjudication trail for compliance

**Member Enrollment Workflow** (5 services, 35-second average duration):
- Member Service creates member profile from state eligibility file
- Eligibility Service activates coverage for plan
- Benefits Service assigns benefit package
- Provider Network Service assigns primary care physician
- Notification Service sends welcome letter and ID card

With 50+ microservices deployed on Kubernetes (AWS EKS), workflows increasingly complex with failures difficult to diagnose. Current monitoring provides service-level metrics (CPU, memory, request rates, error rates per service) but no visibility into end-to-end distributed transactions. When claim processing fails (5-8% failure rate, 75,000-120,000 failures monthly), operations engineers manually correlate logs across 8 services using claim IDs, timestamps, and log aggregation tools—a process taking 2-4 hours per incident.

### Technical Context

**Current Architecture:**
- **Microservices Platform**: 50+ Spring Boot services deployed on AWS EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service)
- **Message Broker**: Apache Kafka (MSK) with 12 topics, 3 partitions per topic, 3 replicas for durability
- **Service Communication**: REST APIs (synchronous) for request-response patterns, Kafka events (asynchronous) for fire-and-forget workflows
- **Logging**: Centralized logging with FluentD → Elasticsearch → Kibana (ELK stack), 500GB daily log volume, 30-day retention
- **Monitoring**: Prometheus for metrics collection, Grafana for visualization, Alertmanager for alerts (service-level metrics only)
- **Service Mesh**: Istio deployed for traffic management, mTLS, and circuit breaking (not currently used for tracing)

**Development Practices:**
- Spring Boot 3.x with Java 17 for new services, Java 11 for legacy services
- Kafka producer/consumer using Spring Kafka library
- Correlation IDs manually generated per service (not propagated consistently across service boundaries)
- Structured logging with JSON format including service name, timestamp, log level, message, but no trace context

**Observability Gaps:**
- No distributed tracing infrastructure (Jaeger or Zipkin not deployed)
- OpenTelemetry not adopted (services lack auto-instrumentation)
- Correlation IDs generated independently per service, not propagated through Kafka event headers
- Flamegraph visualization unavailable (engineers use Kibana logs with manual filtering by timestamp ranges)

#### Problem 1: Inability to Trace End-to-End Workflows Across Service Boundaries

**Scenario**: Claim C123456 submitted through provider portal fails during processing. Provider calls customer service complaining claim "stuck in pending status" for 3 days. Operations engineer investigates by:

1. **Query Claims Service logs** in Kibana: `service:claims-service AND claim_id:C123456`
   - Finds log: `2025-12-20 14:23:15 INFO ClaimReceivedEvent published to Kafka topic:claims-received claim_id:C123456`
   - Confirms claim intake successful

2. **Query Eligibility Service logs**: `service:eligibility-service AND claim_id:C123456`
   - Finds log: `2025-12-20 14:23:18 INFO Consuming ClaimReceivedEvent claim_id:C123456`
   - Finds log: `2025-12-20 14:23:20 ERROR External payer API timeout after 30s claim_id:C123456`
   - Identifies eligibility verification failed due to external API timeout

3. **Query downstream services** (Benefits, Pricing, Payment):
   - No logs found with claim_id:C123456
   - Confirms workflow stopped at eligibility verification

**Time Investment**: 45 minutes to correlate logs across 3 services, identify failure point, and confirm downstream services never executed.

**Root Cause**: Without distributed tracing, engineer must manually reconstruct workflow by querying each service's logs independently using claim ID as correlation key. Process brittle because:
- Not all services log claim ID consistently (some log claim_id, others claimId, ClaimNumber)
- Timestamps across services differ due to clock skew (Claims Service timestamp 14:23:15.234, Eligibility Service 14:23:18.891, unclear if 3.6-second delay is network latency or processing time)
- Kafka consumer lag invisible (did Eligibility Service consume event immediately or after 10-second lag?)

#### Problem 2: Performance Bottlenecks Hidden in Distributed Call Chains

**Scenario**: Claim processing P95 latency degrades from 8 seconds to 18 seconds over 2-week period. Customer service reports provider complaints about "slow claim status updates." Engineering manager tasks team to identify bottleneck.

**Investigation Process**:
1. **Review service-level metrics** in Grafana:
   - Claims Service P95 latency: 150ms (unchanged)
   - Eligibility Service P95 latency: 1.2s (increased from 800ms)
   - Benefits Service P95 latency: 2.5s (unchanged)
   - Pricing Service P95 latency: 4.8s (increased from 2.1s)
   - Payment Service P95 latency: 600ms (unchanged)

2. **Hypothesize pricing service as bottleneck** (4.8s highest latency):
   - Profiler shows pricing service CPU 45%, memory 60% (healthy)
   - Database query logs show 15ms P95 latency (fast)
   - External API calls to fee schedule service show 4.5s P95 latency (root cause!)

3. **Confirm fee schedule service degradation**:
   - Fee schedule service experiencing database contention
   - Pricing service retries fee schedule API 3 times with 1-second backoff
   - Total pricing service latency: 4.5s initial call + 3 retries × (4.5s + 1s backoff) = 20.5s worst case

**Time Investment**: 3 days for 2 engineers to investigate (48 engineer-hours total):
- Day 1: Identify services with elevated latency from Grafana metrics
- Day 2: Profile suspected services, rule out local bottlenecks
- Day 3: Discover external dependency issue through log analysis

**Root Cause**: Service-level metrics show elevated latency but don't reveal which downstream dependency causes delay. Engineers must manually inspect each service's external dependencies (database, Kafka, external APIs, internal service calls) to find bottleneck. Distributed tracing would immediately show fee schedule service consuming 80% of pricing service duration in flamegraph visualization.

#### Problem 3: Cascading Failures Where One Service Impacts Multiple Workflows

**Scenario**: Provider Network Service experiences database connection pool exhaustion due to slow query (30-second query acquiring lock on provider table). Multiple workflows dependent on Provider Network Service start failing simultaneously:
- Claim processing fails at provider verification step (8,000 claims/hour blocked)
- Member enrollment fails at PCP assignment step (500 enrollments/hour blocked)
- Prior authorization fails at provider validation step (300 prior auths/hour blocked)

**Detection**: Alertmanager fires 47 alerts within 5-minute window:
- `HighErrorRate: claim-service error_rate > 5%`
- `HighErrorRate: enrollment-service error_rate > 5%`
- `HighErrorRate: prior-auth-service error_rate > 5%`
- `HighLatency: provider-network-service P95 > 30s`
- ... (43 additional alerts for downstream services experiencing timeouts)

**Diagnosis Challenge**: Operations engineer pages on-call engineer at 2:00 AM. Engineer sees 47 alerts but unclear which is root cause vs. symptom:
- Is provider-network-service slow because of high load from claim-service?
- Is claim-service erroring because provider-network-service is slow?
- Are enrollment-service and prior-auth-service failures independent or related?

Engineer spends 90 minutes:

1. Investigating each service's logs independently
2. Correlating timestamps to determine sequence of failures
3. Identifying provider-network-service database lock as root cause
4. Confirming downstream services timeout waiting for provider-network-service response

**Time Investment**: 90 minutes to identify root cause during incident, followed by 4-hour post-mortem to reconstruct event timeline.

**Root Cause**: Without dependency mapping and trace correlation, engineer can't immediately identify provider-network-service as common dependency for all failing workflows. Distributed tracing with service dependency graphs would show provider-network-service as critical path dependency, enabling immediate root cause identification.

#### Problem 4: Inconsistent Trace Context Propagation Through Kafka Events

**Scenario**: Engineering team adopts best practice of generating correlation IDs for request tracing. Each service generates UUID correlation ID when handling request and includes in log messages. However, correlation IDs not propagated through Kafka event headers:

**Claims Service** (publishes event):
```java
String correlationId = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); // Generate new ID
logger.info("Processing claim correlationId={} claimId={}", correlationId, claimId);
ClaimReceivedEvent event = new ClaimReceivedEvent(claimId, memberData);
kafkaTemplate.send("claims-received", event); // Event does NOT include correlationId
```

**Eligibility Service** (consumes event):
```java
@KafkaListener(topics = "claims-received")
public void handleClaimReceived(ClaimReceivedEvent event) {
    String correlationId = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); // Generate DIFFERENT ID
    logger.info("Received claim correlationId={} claimId={}", correlationId, event.getClaimId());
}
```

**Result**: Claims Service and Eligibility Service log different correlation IDs for same claim processing workflow:
- Claims Service log: `correlationId=a1b2c3d4 claimId=C123456`
- Eligibility Service log: `correlationId=e5f6g7h8 claimId=C123456`

Engineer attempting to trace request flow must rely on claimId instead of correlationId, but claimId only available after claim created (not useful for tracing API Gateway → Claims Service request).

**Root Cause**: Services lack standardized mechanism for propagating trace context through Kafka event headers. OpenTelemetry provides standardized W3C Trace Context format (trace-id, span-id, trace-flags, trace-state) automatically propagated through HTTP headers and Kafka headers with proper instrumentation.

#### Problem 5: Manual Log Correlation Consuming 15-20% of Engineering Time

**Quantified Impact**:
- Team of 10 engineers supporting microservices platform
- Each engineer spends 1-2 hours daily troubleshooting production issues (10-20 hours/engineer/week)
- 60% of troubleshooting time spent correlating logs across services (6-12 hours/engineer/week)
- Total weekly time: 60-120 engineer-hours per week = 240-480 hours monthly = $24K-$48K monthly at $100/hour fully burdened cost

**Common Troubleshooting Patterns**:
1. **API timeout investigation** (30-45 min per incident):
   - Customer reports "claim submission timed out"
   - Engineer queries API Gateway logs for request ID
   - Queries Claims Service logs to confirm request received
   - Queries downstream services (Eligibility, Benefits, Pricing) to identify which service timed out
   - Queries slow service logs to identify root cause (database slow query, external API timeout, high CPU)

2. **Missing data investigation** (60-90 min per incident):
   - Customer service reports "member enrolled but no benefits assigned"
   - Engineer queries Member Service logs confirming member created
   - Queries Eligibility Service logs confirming coverage activated
   - Queries Benefits Service logs showing no record of member ID
   - Checks Kafka topic consumer lag showing Benefits Service 10 minutes behind (cause of missing data)

3. **Duplicate processing investigation** (45-60 min per incident):
   - Finance reports "duplicate payment for claim C123456"
   - Engineer queries Claims Service logs showing claim processed once
   - Queries Payment Service logs showing payment processed twice
   - Analyzes Payment Service code to identify retry logic without idempotency check
   - Reviews Kafka consumer configuration showing missing enable.idempotence setting

**Root Cause**: Engineers spend majority of time manually correlating logs because distributed tracing infrastructure unavailable. Each investigation requires querying multiple services, correlating timestamps, and reconstructing request flow. Distributed tracing would reduce investigation time from 30-90 minutes to 2-5 minutes by providing instant visualization of complete workflow with all spans, timing, and errors in single UI.

### Forces and Constraints

**Observability vs. Cost Trade-offs:**
- **Trace Storage Costs**: Tracing 100% of requests at 1.5M claims/month generates 50-100GB trace data daily, requiring Cassandra cluster ($2K-$3K monthly AWS cost) or Elasticsearch cluster ($3K-$5K monthly)
- **Sampling Trade-offs**: Sampling 5% of successful requests reduces storage to 5-10GB daily ($200-$500 monthly) but risks missing intermittent issues
- **Performance Overhead**: OpenTelemetry instrumentation adds 1-3ms per traced operation, acceptable for asynchronous workflows (claim processing) but potentially impactful for synchronous APIs (member portal page load)

**Engineering Investment vs. Time-to-Value:**
- **Initial Implementation**: 4-6 weeks to deploy Jaeger infrastructure, instrument 50 services with OpenTelemetry, train engineers on distributed tracing (requires 2-3 engineers)
- **Maintenance Overhead**: Ongoing effort to update instrumentation as services evolve, tune sampling strategies, manage trace storage retention
- **Immediate Value**: MTTR reduction from 2-4 hours to 15-30 minutes justifies upfront investment within 3-6 months based on operational cost savings

**Standardization vs. Flexibility:**
- **OpenTelemetry Standard**: Vendor-neutral instrumentation enabling future migration from Jaeger to Datadog/New Relic without re-instrumenting services
- **Custom Instrumentation**: Business-critical spans (claim adjudication logic, eligibility determination) require custom instrumentation beyond auto-instrumentation
- **Adoption Resistance**: Engineering teams may resist adding OpenTelemetry dependencies and propagating trace context through custom code, requires change management

**Real-Time vs. Batch Processing:**
- **Real-Time Workflows**: Distributed tracing provides immediate value for request-response patterns (claim submission, member lookup, provider search)
- **Batch Processing**: Limited value for nightly batch jobs (eligibility file processing, claims reconciliation) better monitored with job-level metrics and logging
- **Hybrid Approach**: Instrument real-time workflows first (80% of troubleshooting effort), defer batch processing instrumentation until real-time workflows stabilized

### Pattern Description

The Infrastructure Event Tracing pattern implements end-to-end distributed tracing for event-driven microservices using **OpenTelemetry** for instrumentation and **Jaeger** for trace collection, storage, and visualization. The solution provides unified visibility into distributed workflows by automatically generating, propagating, and correlating trace context (trace ID, span ID, parent span ID) across service boundaries—both synchronous (REST/gRPC) and asynchronous (Kafka events).

**Core Concepts:**

1. **Trace**: Complete end-to-end journey of a business transaction (e.g., claim processing from submission to payment). Each trace has unique trace ID (128-bit UUID) identifying all operations across services.

2. **Span**: Single unit of work within trace representing one operation (HTTP request, Kafka message production/consumption, database query, external API call). Each span has:
   - Unique span ID (64-bit)
   - Parent span ID (linking to upstream operation)
   - Operation name (e.g., "POST /claims", "process-eligibility-verification")
   - Start timestamp and duration
   - Tags (metadata like http.method=POST, claim.id=C123456)
   - Logs (timestamped events within span like "cache-miss", "retry-attempt-2")
   - Status (OK, ERROR)

3. **Trace Context Propagation**: Mechanism for passing trace context across service boundaries:
   - **HTTP**: W3C Trace Context standard using `traceparent` header (e.g., `00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b9c7c989f97918e1-01`)
   - **Kafka**: Trace context injected into Kafka message headers (traceparent, tracestate)
   - **Service Mesh**: Envoy proxy automatically propagates context for HTTP calls

4. **OpenTelemetry Auto-Instrumentation**: Zero-code instrumentation for common frameworks:
   - Spring Boot: Automatic spans for HTTP server requests, RestTemplate/WebClient calls, JDBC database queries
   - Kafka: Automatic spans for KafkaProducer.send() and @KafkaListener consumption
   - AWS SDK: Automatic spans for S3, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS calls

5. **Custom Instrumentation**: Business-logic spans for domain-specific operations:
   ```java
   Span span = tracer.spanBuilder("adjudicate-claim")
       .setAttribute("claim.id", claimId)
       .setAttribute("claim.amount", claimAmount)
       .startSpan();
   try (Scope scope = span.makeCurrent()) {
       // Business logic
       adjudicationResult = adjudicateClaim(claim);
       span.setAttribute("adjudication.decision", result.getDecision());
   } catch (Exception e) {
       span.recordException(e);
       span.setStatus(StatusCode.ERROR);
       throw e;
   } finally {
       span.end();
   }
   ```

6. **Sampling Strategies**: Control trace volume and costs:
   - **Head-based Sampling**: Decision made at trace creation (sample 100% of errors, 5% of successful requests)
   - **Tail-based Sampling**: Decision made after trace completion (keep all traces with errors or > 10s duration, sample others at 1%)
   - **Adaptive Sampling**: Dynamically adjust sample rate based on traffic volume (high traffic: 1%, low traffic: 20%)

**How It Works:**

1. **Request Initiation**: Client submits claim through API Gateway. API Gateway creates new trace (trace ID = `abc123...`) and root span (span ID = `root001`, operation = "POST /claims"). Trace context injected into HTTP headers passed to Claims Service.

2. **Service Processing**: Claims Service receives request, extracts trace context from HTTP headers, creates child span (span ID = `span001`, parent = `root001`, operation = "ClaimsService.submitClaim"). Service processes claim, publishes ClaimReceivedEvent to Kafka topic, injects trace context into Kafka event headers.

3. **Event Consumption**: Eligibility Service consumes ClaimReceivedEvent from Kafka, extracts trace context from event headers, creates child span (span ID = `span002`, parent = `span001`, operation = "EligibilityService.verifyEligibility"). Service verifies eligibility, publishes EligibilityVerifiedEvent with trace context.

4. **Trace Collection**: Each service exports spans to OpenTelemetry Collector via OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol). Collector batches spans, applies sampling decisions, forwards to Jaeger backend.

5. **Trace Storage**: Jaeger stores complete trace in Cassandra with 30-day retention. Trace searchable by trace ID, service name, operation name, tags (claim.id=C123456), duration range, time range.

6. **Trace Visualization**: Engineer opens Jaeger UI, searches for claim C123456, views flamegraph showing complete workflow: API Gateway (5ms) → Claims Service (150ms) → Eligibility Service (850ms) → Benefits Service (1.2s) → Pricing Service (4.8s) → Payment Service (620ms). Drill into Pricing Service span reveals external API call to fee schedule service taking 4.5s (bottleneck identified).

#### Scenario 1: Successful Claim Processing (End-to-End Trace)

```text
1. Client submits claim via POST /claims
   └─ API Gateway receives request
      ├─ Generate trace_id: abc123-def456-789ghi
      ├─ Create root span: span_id=root001, operation="POST /claims"
      └─ Inject traceparent header: "00-abc123def456789ghi-root001-01"

2. Claims Service receives HTTP request
   └─ Extract trace context from traceparent header
      ├─ trace_id: abc123-def456-789ghi (inherited)
      ├─ Create child span: span_id=claim001, parent=root001
      ├─ operation="ClaimsService.submitClaim"
      ├─ tags: {http.method=POST, claim.id=C123456, claim.amount=5000}
      └─ Process claim intake (validate EDI, parse data, persist to database)

   └─ Publish ClaimReceivedEvent to Kafka
      ├─ Inject trace context into Kafka headers:
      │  - traceparent: "00-abc123def456789ghi-claim001-01"
      │  - tracestate: ""
      └─ KafkaProducer.send() creates automatic span:
         - span_id=kafka001, parent=claim001
         - operation="kafka.send", tags: {kafka.topic=claims-received}

3. Eligibility Service consumes event from Kafka
   └─ Extract trace context from Kafka message headers
      ├─ trace_id: abc123-def456-789ghi (inherited)
      ├─ @KafkaListener creates automatic span:
      │  - span_id=elig001, parent=kafka001
      │  - operation="kafka.consume", tags: {kafka.topic=claims-received}
      └─ Create business logic span: span_id=elig002, parent=elig001
         - operation="EligibilityService.verifyEligibility"
         - tags: {claim.id=C123456, member.id=M789}
         - Call external payer API (creates automatic HTTP client span):
           * span_id=http001, parent=elig002
           * operation="HTTP GET", tags: {http.url=https://payer-api/eligibility}
           * duration=850ms

   └─ Publish EligibilityVerifiedEvent to Kafka (trace context propagated)

4-6. Benefits, Pricing, Payment Services follow same pattern
     └─ Each service extracts trace context from Kafka headers
     └─ Creates spans for business logic and downstream calls
     └─ Publishes events with trace context propagated

7. Complete trace stored in Jaeger:
   Trace ID: abc123-def456-789ghi, Duration: 7.2s, Spans: 42

   Flamegraph:
   [POST /claims] 7.2s (API Gateway)
   └─ [ClaimsService.submitClaim] 150ms
      ├─ [kafka.send] 5ms
      └─ [kafka.consume] 2ms
          └─ [EligibilityService.verifyEligibility] 920ms
              ├─ [HTTP GET /eligibility] 850ms ← Bottleneck identified
              ├─ [kafka.send] 4ms
              └─ [kafka.consume] 2ms
                  └─ [BenefitsService.calculateBenefits] 1.3s
                      └─ ... (continues through Payment, Notification)
```

#### Variation 1: Service Mesh Auto-Tracing (Istio/Envoy)

**Use Case**: Organizations using Istio service mesh can enable automatic trace propagation for HTTP calls without instrumenting application code.

**Implementation**:
- Istio Envoy proxies intercept all HTTP traffic between services
- Envoy automatically injects `traceparent` headers into requests
- Envoy generates spans for service-to-service HTTP calls
- Application code only needs to propagate trace context (not create spans)

**Benefits**:
- Zero-code instrumentation for HTTP tracing
- Consistent tracing across polyglot services (Java, Python, .NET, Go)
- Service dependency graphs automatically generated from observed traffic

**Limitations**:
- Only traces HTTP traffic (Kafka events still require OpenTelemetry instrumentation)
- Less visibility into business logic (spans represent HTTP calls, not domain operations)
- Service mesh overhead (additional latency from proxy, resource consumption)

**Configuration**:
```yaml
# Istio ConfigMap
meshConfig:
  enableTracing: true
  defaultConfig:
    tracing:
      sampling: 5.0  # 5% sampling
      zipkin:
        address: jaeger-collector.observability:9411
```

#### Variation 2: Tail-Based Sampling (Cost Optimization)

**Use Case**: High-volume services generating millions of traces daily need cost-effective sampling while preserving traces for errors and slow requests.

**Implementation**:
- Head-based sampling at service level: 1% of all requests
- Tail-based sampling at OpenTelemetry Collector: Keep ALL traces with:
  - HTTP status >= 500 (errors)
  - Duration > 10 seconds (slow requests)
  - Custom attribute "sampling.priority=1" (business-critical workflows)
- Effective sampling: 1% of successful fast requests + 100% of errors/slow requests

**Benefits**:
- Reduce storage costs by 90-95% (keep only actionable traces)
- Guarantee all production issues captured (100% error trace retention)
- Preserve performance investigation capability (100% slow trace retention)

**Configuration**:
```yaml
# OpenTelemetry Collector
processors:
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 10s
    policies:
      - name: errors
        type: status_code
        status_code: {status_codes: [ERROR]}
      - name: slow-requests
        type: latency
        latency: {threshold_ms: 10000}
      - name: business-critical
        type: string_attribute
        string_attribute: {key: sampling.priority, values: ["1"]}
      - name: sample-others
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic: {sampling_percentage: 1}
```

#### Variation 3: Multi-Backend Export (Hybrid Observability)

**Use Case**: Organizations using commercial APM tools (Datadog, New Relic) want distributed tracing without vendor lock-in.

**Implementation**:
- OpenTelemetry Collector exports traces to multiple backends simultaneously:
  - Jaeger (self-hosted, detailed debugging, 30-day retention)
  - Datadog (APM + metrics + logs correlation, 15-day retention, $15/host/month)
- Services instrumented once with OpenTelemetry (vendor-neutral)
- Switch backends without re-instrumenting services

**Benefits**:
- Avoid vendor lock-in (standardize on OpenTelemetry)
- Combine strengths of multiple tools (Jaeger deep debugging + Datadog unified observability)
- Evaluate new tools without migration risk

**Configuration**:
```yaml
# OpenTelemetry Collector
exporters:
  jaeger:
    endpoint: jaeger-collector:14250
    tls:
      insecure: true

  datadog:
    api:
      key: ${DD_API_KEY}
      site: datadoghq.com

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [jaeger, datadog]  # Export to both
```

### Prerequisites

**Infrastructure Requirements:**
- Kubernetes cluster (AWS EKS, Azure AKS, or GKE) with 10+ nodes for running microservices and observability infrastructure
- Cassandra cluster (3-5 nodes) or Elasticsearch cluster for Jaeger trace storage:
  - Cassandra: 500GB-1TB SSD storage per node, 16GB RAM minimum per node
  - Elasticsearch: 3 data nodes with 100GB-200GB SSD per node, 32GB RAM per node
- OpenTelemetry Collector deployed as Kubernetes DaemonSet (1 collector pod per node) or centralized Deployment
- Jaeger Operator installed in Kubernetes cluster for managing Jaeger components

**Technology Stack:**
- Spring Boot 3.x with Java 17+ (for new services) or Java 11+ (for legacy services)
- OpenTelemetry Java Agent 1.32+ or OpenTelemetry Java SDK 1.32+
- Apache Kafka 3.x with Spring Kafka 3.x for event-driven communication
- Jaeger 1.50+ (latest stable release)
- Optional: Istio 1.19+ or Linkerd 2.14+ for service mesh auto-tracing

**Skills and Knowledge:**
- Understanding of distributed tracing concepts (traces, spans, trace context propagation)
- Familiarity with OpenTelemetry instrumentation (auto-instrumentation vs. manual instrumentation)
- Experience with Kubernetes deployments (Helm charts, operators, resource configuration)
- Knowledge of Kafka message headers for trace context propagation
- Basic understanding of observability backends (metrics, logs, traces correlation)

**Organizational Readiness:**
- Engineering team commitment to instrument services (2-4 weeks effort for 50 services with 2-3 engineers)
- Budget approval for observability infrastructure ($3K-$5K monthly AWS costs for Cassandra + OpenTelemetry Collectors + Jaeger)
- Change management plan for adopting new troubleshooting workflows (engineers must learn Jaeger UI, distributed tracing concepts)
- Stakeholder buy-in for performance overhead (1-3ms latency per traced operation acceptable)

#### Phase 1: Infrastructure Setup (Week 1-2)

**Week 1: Deploy Jaeger Backend and Storage**

1. **Provision Cassandra cluster** for trace storage (recommended for production scale):
   ```bash
   # Deploy Cassandra using Helm
   helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
   helm install cassandra bitnami/cassandra \
     --namespace observability --create-namespace \
     --set replicaCount=3 \
     --set persistence.size=500Gi \
     --set resources.requests.memory=16Gi \
     --set resources.requests.cpu=4
   ```

2. **Install Jaeger Operator** in Kubernetes:
   ```bash
   kubectl create namespace observability
   kubectl create -f https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger-operator/releases/download/v1.50.0/jaeger-operator.yaml -n observability
   ```

3. **Deploy Jaeger Production instance** with Cassandra backend:
   ```yaml
   # jaeger-production.yaml
   apiVersion: jaegertracing.io/v1
   kind: Jaeger
   metadata:
     name: jaeger-production
     namespace: observability
   spec:
     strategy: production
     storage:
       type: cassandra
       options:
         cassandra:
           servers: cassandra.observability.svc.cluster.local
           keyspace: jaeger_v1_dc1
           replication-factor: 3
       cassandraCreateSchema:
         enabled: true
         datacenter: dc1
     ingester:
       options:
         kafka:
           topic: jaeger-spans
           brokers: kafka.kafka.svc.cluster.local:9092
     collector:
       resources:
         limits:
           memory: 2Gi
           cpu: 1000m
         requests:
           memory: 1Gi
           cpu: 500m
       replicas: 3
     query:
       resources:
         limits:
           memory: 1Gi
           cpu: 500m
       replicas: 2
   ```

   Apply: `kubectl apply -f jaeger-production.yaml`

4. **Expose Jaeger UI** via Ingress or LoadBalancer:
   ```yaml
   # jaeger-ingress.yaml
   apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
   kind: Ingress
   metadata:
     name: jaeger-ui
     namespace: observability
     annotations:
       cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
   spec:
     ingressClassName: nginx
     tls:
       - hosts:
           - jaeger.example.com
         secretName: jaeger-tls
     rules:
       - host: jaeger.example.com
         http:
           paths:
             - path: /
               pathType: Prefix
               backend:
                 service:
                   name: jaeger-production-query
                   port:
                     number: 16686
   ```

**Week 2: Deploy OpenTelemetry Collector**

1. **Create OpenTelemetry Collector ConfigMap**:
   ```yaml
   # otel-collector-config.yaml
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: ConfigMap
   metadata:
     name: otel-collector-config
     namespace: observability
   data:
     otel-collector-config.yaml: |
       receivers:
         otlp:
           protocols:
             grpc:
               endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
             http:
               endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

       processors:
         batch:
           timeout: 10s
           send_batch_size: 1024

         memory_limiter:
           check_interval: 1s
           limit_mib: 512

         tail_sampling:
           decision_wait: 10s
           policies:
             - name: errors
               type: status_code
               status_code:
                 status_codes: [ERROR]
             - name: slow-requests
               type: latency
               latency:
                 threshold_ms: 5000
             - name: sample-successful
               type: probabilistic
               probabilistic:
                 sampling_percentage: 5

       exporters:
         jaeger:
           endpoint: jaeger-production-collector.observability:14250
           tls:
             insecure: true

         logging:
           loglevel: debug

       service:
         pipelines:
           traces:
             receivers: [otlp]
             processors: [memory_limiter, tail_sampling, batch]
             exporters: [jaeger, logging]
   ```

2. **Deploy OpenTelemetry Collector as DaemonSet**:
   ```yaml
   # otel-collector-daemonset.yaml
   apiVersion: apps/v1
   kind: DaemonSet
   metadata:
     name: otel-collector
     namespace: observability
   spec:
     selector:
       matchLabels:
         app: otel-collector
     template:
       metadata:
         labels:
           app: otel-collector
       spec:
         containers:
           - name: otel-collector
             image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.91.0
             args:
               - --config=/conf/otel-collector-config.yaml
             ports:
               - containerPort: 4317  # OTLP gRPC
               - containerPort: 4318  # OTLP HTTP
             volumeMounts:
               - name: otel-collector-config
                 mountPath: /conf
             resources:
               limits:
                 memory: 512Mi
                 cpu: 500m
               requests:
                 memory: 256Mi
                 cpu: 250m
         volumes:
           - name: otel-collector-config
             configMap:
               name: otel-collector-config
   ---
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Service
   metadata:
     name: otel-collector
     namespace: observability
   spec:
     selector:
       app: otel-collector
     ports:
       - name: otlp-grpc
         port: 4317
         targetPort: 4317
       - name: otlp-http
         port: 4318
         targetPort: 4318
   ```

3. **Verify infrastructure deployment**:
   ```bash
   # Check Jaeger components
   kubectl get pods -n observability -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=jaeger-production

   # Check OpenTelemetry Collector
   kubectl get pods -n observability -l app=otel-collector

   # Access Jaeger UI
   kubectl port-forward -n observability svc/jaeger-production-query 16686:16686
   # Open http://localhost:16686
   ```

#### Phase 4: Production Rollout (Week 7-8)

**Week 7: Canary Deployment**

1. **Deploy instrumented services to 10% of traffic**:

1. **Deploy instrumented services to 100% of traffic**
2. **Conduct engineer training** (2-hour session):
   - Jaeger UI navigation (search, trace detail, flamegraph, service dependencies)
   - Troubleshooting workflows (finding root cause of failures, identifying bottlenecks)
   - Custom span creation for business logic visibility
   - Trace context propagation best practices
3. **Update runbooks** to include distributed tracing in incident response procedures

### Best Practices

**Instrumentation Best Practices:**
- Use OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation for common frameworks (Spring Boot, Kafka, JDBC) to minimize code changes
- Add custom spans only for business-critical operations requiring visibility (claim adjudication, eligibility determination, pricing calculations)
- Include business context as span attributes (claim.id, member.id, provider.id) for searchability in Jaeger
- Record exceptions in spans using `span.recordException(e)` to preserve stack traces
- Use span events (`span.addEvent("cache-miss")`) for significant milestones within operations

**Trace Context Propagation:**
- Always propagate trace context through Kafka message headers using W3C Trace Context format
- Extract trace context in Kafka consumers before processing messages
- Propagate trace context through external API calls (REST, gRPC) using HTTP headers
- Use consistent propagator configuration (W3C Trace Context) across all services

**Sampling Strategies:**
- Start with 100% sampling during initial rollout to validate instrumentation (1-2 weeks)
- Reduce to 5-10% sampling for high-volume services after validation
- Always trace 100% of errors (status=ERROR) and slow requests (> 5-10 seconds)
- Use tail-based sampling at OpenTelemetry Collector to preserve important traces while reducing storage costs

**Performance Optimization:**
- Batch span exports (10-second batch window) to reduce network overhead
- Limit span attributes to essential business context (< 20 attributes per span)
- Avoid creating spans in tight loops (e.g., span per item in batch processing)
- Use asynchronous span export to avoid blocking request processing

**Operational Best Practices:**
- Set up alerts for trace export failures (> 1% failure rate indicates collector issues)
- Monitor OpenTelemetry Collector resource usage (CPU, memory) and scale as needed
- Configure trace storage retention based on compliance requirements (30 days typical, 90 days for HIPAA)
- Create team runbooks documenting Jaeger UI workflows for common troubleshooting scenarios

### Common Pitfalls

**Pitfall 1: Not Propagating Trace Context Through Kafka**
- **Problem**: Services generate independent traces instead of single end-to-end trace because trace context not included in Kafka message headers
- **Impact**: Cannot visualize complete workflow in flamegraph, manual correlation required
- **Avoidance**: Always inject trace context into Kafka headers on producer side, extract on consumer side using W3C Trace Context Propagator

**Pitfall 2: Over-Instrumentation Creating Performance Overhead**
- **Problem**: Creating spans for every method call or database query generates excessive span volume (> 1000 spans per trace), causing 10-20ms latency overhead and storage costs
- **Impact**: Unacceptable performance degradation, high Cassandra storage costs
- **Avoidance**: Create spans only for coarse-grained operations (service boundaries, external API calls, business logic methods). Let auto-instrumentation handle fine-grained operations (database queries, HTTP requests).

**Pitfall 3: Missing Business Context in Span Attributes**
- **Problem**: Spans lack business identifiers (claim ID, member ID), making traces unsearchable by business context
- **Impact**: Cannot find specific claim processing trace in Jaeger, must resort to timestamp-based search
- **Avoidance**: Always add business identifiers as span attributes: `span.setAttribute("claim.id", claimId)`, `span.setAttribute("member.id", memberId)`

**Pitfall 4: Not Recording Exceptions in Spans**
- **Problem**: Service logs exception but doesn't record in span, trace shows success status despite failure
- **Impact**: Jaeger UI doesn't highlight failed traces, engineers miss critical errors
- **Avoidance**: Always call `span.recordException(e)` and `span.setStatus(StatusCode.ERROR)` in exception handlers

**Pitfall 5: Insufficient Sampling Leading to Missed Issues**
- **Problem**: Aggressive sampling (0.1%) to reduce costs results in missing intermittent issues occurring in < 1% of requests
- **Impact**: Cannot investigate production issues because trace not sampled
- **Avoidance**: Use tail-based sampling to keep 100% of error traces and slow traces while sampling successful traces at lower rate. Start with 5% sampling minimum.

**Pitfall 6: Not Configuring Trace Storage Retention**
- **Problem**: Default Cassandra retention (7 days) insufficient for long-running investigations or compliance audits
- **Impact**: Historical traces deleted before investigation complete
- **Avoidance**: Configure Cassandra TTL to 30-90 days based on compliance requirements. Monitor storage growth and costs.

**Pitfall 7: Ignoring OpenTelemetry Collector Resource Limits**
- **Problem**: Collector runs out of memory or CPU under high load, drops spans silently
- **Impact**: Incomplete traces in Jaeger, cannot debug production issues
- **Avoidance**: Set resource limits (memory, CPU) for collectors, monitor collector metrics (spans received, spans dropped, export errors), scale collectors horizontally as traffic grows

### Standards Alignment

**Observability Standards:**
- **[Logging Standard](../../technology/observability/logging-standard.md)** (STD-TECH-LOG-001): Distributed tracing complements structured logging by correlating logs across services using trace IDs. Services emit logs with trace_id and span_id attributes, enabling correlation in Kibana. Recommendation: Include trace context in all log messages using MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) for automatic injection.

- **[Monitoring Standard](../../technology/observability/monitoring-standard.md)** (STD-TECH-MON-001): Distributed tracing extends service-level monitoring by providing request-level visibility. Prometheus metrics show aggregate service health (error rate, latency percentiles), while Jaeger traces show individual request flows.

- **[Event-Driven Architecture Standard](../../technology/integration/event-driven-architecture-standard.md)** (STD-TECH-EDA-001): Trace context must propagate through Kafka events following W3C Trace Context format. Services publishing events inject traceparent header, consumers extract to continue trace.

**Infrastructure Standards:**
- **[Kubernetes Deployment Standard](../../infrastructure/container/kubernetes-deployment-standard.md)** (STD-INFRA-K8S-001): OpenTelemetry Collector deployed as DaemonSet (1 collector per node) following standard resource limits, monitoring, and high availability requirements.

- **[Service Mesh Standard](../../infrastructure/service-mesh/service-mesh-standard.md)** (STD-INFRA-MESH-001): For organizations with Istio service mesh, leverage Envoy proxy automatic trace propagation for HTTP traffic.

**Security Standards:**
- **[Data Protection Standard](../../security/data/data-protection-standard.md)** (STD-SEC-DATA-001): Trace spans must not include PHI (Protected Health Information) in span attributes or events. Use identifiers (claim ID, member ID) instead of sensitive data.

### Compliance Requirements

**HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act):**
- **Audit Trail Requirements** (45 CFR § 164.312(b)): Distributed tracing provides complete audit trail for PHI access across microservices. Every span touching PHI must include user identity, access timestamp, operation performed, data accessed, access result.
- **Retention Requirements**: Traces containing PHI access must retain for 6 years per HIPAA requirements. Configure Cassandra TTL accordingly.
- **Encryption Requirements**: Traces transmitted over network must use TLS 1.2+. Traces stored in Cassandra must use encryption at rest.

**SOC 2 Type II:**
- **Availability**: Distributed tracing infrastructure must meet 99.9% availability SLA.
- **Processing Integrity**: Trace data must accurately represent system behavior.
- **Confidentiality**: Access to trace data restricted to authorized personnel.

**21 CFR Part 11 (FDA Electronic Records):**
- For healthcare organizations subject to FDA regulations, distributed traces may constitute electronic records requiring audit trail, data integrity, and electronic signatures for exports.

### Real-World Example 1: Claim Processing Workflow Debugging

**Context**: Healthcare payer processing 1.5M claims monthly experiences 5-8% failure rate (75K-120K failures). Operations team spends 2-4 hours per incident manually correlating logs across 8 microservices (Claims, Eligibility, Benefits, Pricing, Provider Network, Payment, Notification, Audit) to identify root cause of failures.

**Implementation**:
1. **Deployed Jaeger infrastructure** (Week 1-2): Cassandra 3-node cluster (500GB per node), Jaeger Operator managing collector/query/ingester components, OpenTelemetry Collector as DaemonSet, Jaeger UI exposed via Ingress with OAuth authentication
2. **Instrumented services** (Week 3-6): Added OpenTelemetry Spring Boot Starter to all 8 services, configured OTLP exporter, implemented custom spans for business logic, propagated trace context through Kafka message headers using W3C Trace Context format
3. **Configured tail-based sampling** (Week 7): 100% of error traces, 100% of slow traces (> 10 seconds), 5% of successful traces, reduced storage costs by 90%

**Outcome**:
- **MTTR reduced 85%**: 2-4 hours → 15-30 minutes (engineer searches Jaeger for failing claim, flamegraph immediately shows eligibility service span with SocketTimeoutException from external payer API, root cause identified in 2 minutes vs. 45 minutes manual log correlation)
- **Troubleshooting time reduced 80%**: 45-90 minutes → 5-15 minutes per incident (single Jaeger query shows complete workflow vs. querying Claims, Eligibility, Benefits logs separately)
- **Engineering productivity improved**: 15-20% time on troubleshooting → 6-8% (10 engineers × 6-10 hours/week saved = $24K-$40K monthly cost savings at $100/hour)
- **Proactive performance optimization**: Flamegraph analysis revealed pricing service consuming 60% of total claim processing time, investigation showed external fee schedule API taking 4.5 seconds (bottleneck), implemented fee schedule caching, reduced P95 from 12s → 6s (50% improvement)
- **Dependency mapping**: Jaeger automatically generated service dependency graph showing claims service depends on 7 downstream services, identified provider network service as critical path dependency for 3 workflows (claims, enrollment, prior auth)

### Real-World Example 2: Cascading Failure Root Cause Analysis

**Context**: Provider Network Service database connection pool exhausted due to slow query (30-second lock). Multiple workflows failed simultaneously (claims processing, member enrollment, prior authorization), triggering 47 alerts. On-call engineer paged at 2:00 AM needs to identify root cause quickly.

**Implementation**:
1. Engineer opens Jaeger UI, searches for traces in last 10 minutes with status=error
2. Identifies pattern: 50+ traces spanning 3 different workflows all showing timeouts calling provider-network-service
3. Drills into single trace showing Claims service span with HTTP timeout after 30 seconds calling provider-network-service GET /providers/{id}
4. Checks service dependency graph confirming provider-network-service as common dependency for all 3 failing workflows
5. Investigates provider-network-service traces showing internal spans with database query taking 30 seconds (normally < 50ms), query logs reveal database lock acquired on provider table

**Outcome**:
- **Root cause identified in 10 minutes** (vs. 90 minutes manual investigation): Provider Network Service database lock caused cascading failures across 3 workflows, immediate remediation (kill slow query, restart connection pool), permanent fix (add database query timeout, optimize query with missing index)
- **Reduced blast radius**: Distributed tracing enabled quick isolation of root cause service, only provider-network-service restarted (vs. restarting all 50 services), workflows resumed within 5 minutes
- **Prevented future incidents**: Trace analysis revealed slow query pattern affecting 3 critical workflows, engineering team prioritized database query optimization, added monitoring for database query duration

### Related Patterns

**Prerequisites (Required):**
- **[Logging Standard](../../technology/observability/logging-standard.md)** (STD-TECH-LOG-001) - Distributed tracing complements structured logging by correlating logs across services using trace IDs. Services must emit structured logs with trace_id and span_id for correlation in Kibana. Implement logging standard before adding distributed tracing to ensure log quality.

- **[Event-Driven Architecture Pattern](../messaging/application-event-driven-architecture-pattern.md)** (PTN-APP-EDA-001) - Services must publish and consume events via message broker (Kafka). Distributed tracing propagates trace context through Kafka message headers, enabling end-to-end visibility across asynchronous workflows. EDA pattern establishes event-driven communication, tracing pattern adds observability.

**Complementary Patterns (Enhance this pattern):**
- **[Monitoring and Alerting Pattern](../observability/infrastructure-monitoring-alerting-pattern.md)** (PTN-INFRA-MON-001) - Prometheus metrics provide aggregate service health (error rate, latency percentiles), while Jaeger traces show individual request flows. Combined: Prometheus alert fires for high error rate, engineers use Jaeger to investigate specific failing requests. Metrics identify "what" is failing, traces identify "why."

- **[Centralized Logging Pattern](../observability/infrastructure-centralized-logging-pattern.md)** (PTN-INFRA-LOG-001) - ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) aggregates logs from all services. Distributed tracing adds trace_id to logs, enabling correlation in Kibana. Engineer searches Jaeger for trace, extracts trace_id, queries Kibana for all logs with matching trace_id to see detailed log messages alongside trace spans.

- **[API Gateway Pattern](../integration/application-api-gateway-pattern.md)** (PTN-APP-APIGW-001) - API Gateway serves as entry point for all client requests, ideal location for generating trace IDs and creating root spans. Gateway injects trace context into requests forwarded to backend services, ensuring all downstream operations inherit same trace.

- **[Service Mesh Pattern](../infrastructure/infrastructure-service-mesh-pattern.md)** (PTN-INFRA-MESH-001) - Istio/Linkerd Envoy proxies automatically propagate trace context for HTTP traffic without code changes. Service mesh provides zero-code instrumentation for HTTP tracing, complementing OpenTelemetry instrumentation for Kafka events and business logic.

- **[Circuit Breaker Pattern](../resilience/application-circuit-breaker-pattern.md)** (PTN-APP-CB-001) - Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures by failing fast when downstream services unavailable. Distributed tracing reveals which service triggered circuit breaker (span shows CircuitBreakerOpenException), helping engineers identify root cause of cascading failures.

**Alternative Patterns (Different approaches):**
- **[Application Performance Monitoring (APM) Pattern](../observability/infrastructure-apm-pattern.md)** (PTN-INFRA-APM-001) - Commercial APM tools (Datadog APM, New Relic, AppDynamics) provide distributed tracing, metrics, and logs in unified platform. Alternative to self-hosted Jaeger with lower operational burden but higher cost ($15-$50/host/month) and potential vendor lock-in. Choose Jaeger for cost-effectiveness and vendor neutrality, APM for integrated observability and managed service.

- **[Correlation ID Pattern](../observability/application-correlation-id-pattern.md)** (PTN-APP-CORR-001) - Simple correlation ID (UUID) propagated through HTTP headers and Kafka messages enables log correlation without distributed tracing infrastructure. Lighter-weight alternative suitable for small microservices deployments (< 5 services) where full distributed tracing overhead not justified. Upgrade to distributed tracing when manual log correlation becomes time-consuming.

Not applicable to monolithic applications where single-process tracing (profilers, APM) more appropriate.

## TL;DR

**Problem:** Distributed event-driven microservices architectures (50+ services) lack end-to-end request tracing, causing high mean time to resolution (2-4 hours) for production incidents. Engineers manually correlate logs across services (15-20% of engineering time), performance bottlenecks remain hidden in multi-hop request flows, and cascading failures difficult to diagnose due to lack of service dependency visibility.

**Solution:** Instrument services with OpenTelemetry SDK for automatic trace context propagation, deploy Jaeger backend for trace collection and visualization. Trace ID and span ID injected at API Gateway, propagated through all service calls (REST APIs and Kafka events), collected by OpenTelemetry Collector, stored in Cassandra/Elasticsearch, and visualized in Jaeger UI with flamegraphs showing complete request flow and latency breakdown.

**When to Use:** Event-driven microservices architectures with 5+ services, complex multi-hop request flows spanning multiple services and message queues, performance troubleshooting requiring latency breakdown per service, production incident resolution needing fast root cause analysis, compliance requirements for audit trails showing complete request processing path.

**Key Benefits:**
- 75% reduction in mean time to resolution (2-4 hours → 30 minutes)
- 60% reduction in troubleshooting time (15-20% → 5-8% of engineering time)
- Proactive performance bottleneck identification via P95/P99 latency analysis
- Automated service dependency mapping showing impact radius of failures
- Complete compliance audit trails for regulatory requirements (HIPAA, SOC 2)

**Implementation Complexity:** Medium - 11-15 weeks total implementation (infrastructure setup 2 weeks, first service instrumentation 1-2 weeks, service-by-service rollout 4-6 weeks, production optimization 2-3 weeks). Requires 3-4 developers with distributed systems expertise, Kubernetes cluster for Jaeger deployment, Cassandra/Elasticsearch for trace storage.

**Prerequisites:** Microservices architecture with 5+ independently deployable services, Kubernetes cluster (10+ nodes recommended) for deploying Jaeger and OpenTelemetry Collectors, Kafka or other message broker for event-driven communication, engineering team skilled in distributed systems concepts and observability practices, structured logging standard already implemented (STD-TECH-LOG-001).

**Related Patterns:** Event-Driven Architecture Pattern (PTN-APP-EDA-001) provides event infrastructure for trace propagation, Microservices Architecture Pattern (STD-APP-MICRO-001) establishes service boundaries requiring distributed tracing, Monitoring and Alerting Pattern (PTN-INFRA-MON-001) provides metrics complementing trace data, API Gateway Pattern (PTN-APP-APIGW-001) generates initial trace IDs, Service Mesh Pattern (PTN-INFRA-MESH-001) provides zero-code HTTP tracing.
